For most U.S. household refrigerators, I recommend a 1,000–2,000 Wh (1–2 kWh) portable power station with at least 1,200–1,500 W of surge capacity and a pure sine wave inverter. Choose closer to 2,000 Wh if you want to keep food cold through a full day or longer outage.

The right size depends on how long you need the refrigerator to run and its compressor’s startup surge.

What size do you need?

Short outages: 500–1,000 Wh

Several hours

Suitable for shorter outages or efficient, smaller refrigerators. Check the surge rating carefully; not every small unit can start a full-size fridge.

Around one day: 1,000–1,500 Wh

Good starting point

A practical choice for many refrigerators. The BLUETTI AC180 has 1,152 Wh capacity, 1,800 W continuous output and 2,700 W peak output.

Estimated runtime varies; a 1,000 Wh-class unit may not last a full 24 hours.

A full day or longer: 2,000 Wh

My recommendation

The BLUETTI AC200L offers 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous AC output and a 3,600 W Power Lifting rating. It is expandable for longer outages.

The three specifications to check

Continuous output (W): A typical full-size refrigerator may draw about 100–250 W while its compressor runs.

Surge output (W): The station must handle the brief compressor startup demand. A planning target of at least 1,200 W is reasonable, but check your fridge's actual requirements.

Battery capacity (Wh): This determines how long it runs. A typical full-size fridge may need around 1,400 Wh of rated battery capacity for 24 hours when conversion losses and a reserve are included, according to PowerStations Reviews.

Choose a pure sine wave AC output, and remember that running additional appliances reduces runtime.
